data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'risk-management' strategy: we prefer the theory with the highest informational content that has survived severe tests, not because it is more likely true, but because it offers the greatest potential for future falsification and learning while currently being the least error-prone known option.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent prefers the theory because they believe it will *continue* to work (future reliability), this collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'better corroborated' implicitly relies on a frequency count of past successes rather than the severity of tests passed.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Corroboration reports the historical survival of high-content (improbable) theories. Preferring them maximizes the 'boldness' of our current stance without asserting probability. It is a rule of action based on the logical status of the theory (high content + survived) rather than an inductive inference about its future reliability.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
